extracted.intended_audience: writers, editors, and copyeditors working in English
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and prescriptive rules for grammar and usage in written English, intended to help writers and editors produce clear, standard, and publishable prose. Covers parts of speech, noun and pronoun behavior, case, number, plurals, appositives, and functional shifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common vs. Proper Nouns — capitalization and use
rubrics_metrics.description: A common noun names a generic class or type and is not capitalized unless it begins a sentence or appears in a title; a proper noun names a specific person, place, or thing and is always capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common nouns are usually used with a determiner and may be concrete, abstract, or collective. Proper nouns may be singular or plural and retain capitalization even in different sentence positions. Some common nouns can become proper nouns over time; some proper nouns may be used figuratively as common nouns. Examples: {a chemist} vs {John Doe}; {Citizen Kane}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mass (noncount) nouns — article and agreement behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass nouns denote uncountable aggregations or abstractities and typically do not take indefinite articles or plural forms; as subjects they usually take singular verbs and pronouns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mass nouns can appear alone or with determiners other than an indefinite article (some music, the music). Some mass nouns are plural in form but singular in use (politics, news), and a few plural-form words are always treated as plural (manners, scissors). Use unit nouns (a piece of, a pair of) to enumerate mass nouns when needed. Examples: {music is}, {a piece of stationery}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plural-form words with singular sense — usage guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Words plural in form (data, media, economics) may be used with singular or plural verbs depending on tradition and register; in the sciences data is always plural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In formal contexts, retain traditional plural uses unless they seem artificial; consider alternative words (information, journalists) or adopt the newer singular usage but be consistent. Examples: {the data are inconclusive} (traditional) vs {the data shows} (newer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plural treatment of proper and collective nouns by dialect
rubrics_metrics.description: Plural geographical names or collective nouns are often treated as singular in American English but may take plural verbs in British English when referring to groups of individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: American English: {General Motors reports that it will earn a profit}. British English: {Manchester United have won the FIFA Cup}. Choose dialectal convention appropriate to the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plural formation — consult dictionary for exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Basic plural rules exist but many exceptions abound; use a reliable dictionary or usage guide to check standard plural forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some nouns have irregular plurals (mouse → mice), some are plural-only or singular-only; some plural words (people → peoples) have extended senses. When in doubt, check reference sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noun case functions (nominative, objective, genitive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Case denotes the relationship between a noun (or pronoun) and other words: nominative for subjects/predicate nominatives, objective for direct/indirect objects and objects of prepositions, genitive for ownership/relationship/agency/description/roles/idiomatic of-phrases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nominative usually precedes and controls the verb; objective usually follows verb or preposition and does not control verb number; genitive formed by -'s or apostrophe depending on noun(s) and function. See examples: {the governor delivered a speech} (nominative), {place the slide under the microscope} (objective), {the architect’s drawing board} (genitive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Genitive formation and choice with of-construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Use -'s for singular and many plural genitives, use an apostrophe after s for plural nouns ending in s, and consider of-construction for inanimate nouns or where style favors it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper nouns and nouns denoting people or higher-status entities usually take the inflected genitive ({Hilda’s adventures}); inanimate nouns often accept either form ({the theater’s name} / {the name of the theater}), but some feel right only in of-form ({the end of everything}). Double genitives (an idea of Hill’s) and compound-noun genitives (parents-in-law’s message) follow stated rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint vs. separate genitives (possession clarity)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two or more nouns share possession, only the final noun takes the genitive; if they possess separately, each noun takes a genitive ending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: {Peter and Harriet’s correspondence} (joint; correspondence between them) vs {Peter’s and Harriet’s correspondence} (separate; each has distinct correspondence). If a noun and pronoun express joint possession, both should show possession ({Hilda’s and his vacation}).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appositives — restrictive vs. nonrestrictive punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: An appositive immediately follows a noun to define or further identify it; nonrestrictive appositives are set off by commas, restrictive appositives are not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A restrictive appositive is essential to identity and cannot be removed without losing meaning ({the poet Robert Burns}); a nonrestrictive appositive adds information and is comma-framed ({George Washington, our first president, ...}).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nouns used attributively (nouns as adjectives)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a noun modifies another noun (attributive noun), it typically appears in singular form and functions like an adjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attributive nouns can create ambiguity (fast results = rapid results or results of a fast?). Sometimes a preposition would clarify meaning; context affects interpretation. Examples: {car dealership} (not cars dealership), {state legislature}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denominal verbs (nouns as verbs) — caution in formal prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Nouns commonly become verbs (denominal verbs), but newly transformed or jargon-derived noun-to-verb usages should be used cautiously in formal writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historic examples show naturalization of such verbs, but in formal contexts prefer established forms; e.g., mainstream → mainstreaming appears in some contexts but may be unsuitable in formal prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adverbial uses of nouns (adverbial objectives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinarily nouns can function adverbially when a preposition is omitted (we rode single file); this is traditional and sometimes called an adverbial objective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such shifts usually occur by omission of a preposition ({Sam walked home} from {Sam walked to his home}). These constructions can also modify adjectives ({the team is four members strong}).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pronouns — antecedent clarity requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A pronoun typically refers to an antecedent (earlier noun/pronoun/phrase/clause) and that antecedent should be explicit and clear to avoid ambiguity or miscue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambiguity arises from missing antecedents ({the clown’s act with his dog made it a pleasure...}), multiple possible antecedents ({Scott visited Eric after his discharge...}) or multiple pronouns/antecedents in a sentence. Writers should ensure antecedents are unambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable pronouns without antecedents
rubrics_metrics.description: Some pronouns do not require antecedents: first-person (I, we), second-person (you) in direct address, expletives (there, it), interrogative/relative pronouns (who, what) and certain phrasal pronouns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These pronouns can stand without explicit antecedents ({Are you bringing your boots?}, {It is too hot}, {who cares what I think?}). In colloquial usage unspecified pronouns (they) appear without antecedents but may invite skepticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pronoun properties and agreement (number, person, gender, case)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pronouns have four properties—number, person, gender, and case—and a pronoun must agree with its antecedent in number, person, and gender (pronoun-antecedent agreement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only third-person singular pronouns can display number, person, and gender simultaneously; second-person you no longer shows singular/plural distinction. Ensure agreement in number and gender when selecting pronoun forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pronoun number rules with collective and compound antecedents
rubrics_metrics.description: Pronoun number is guided by the antecedent: collective nouns take singular pronouns if treated as a unit, plural if members act individually; compound antecedents joined by and take plural pronouns; special rules apply when antecedents are joined by each/every/either-or/etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and refinements: collective — {the audience showed its appreciation} vs {the audience rushed back to their seats}; compound — {the boy and girl left their bicycles}. When antecedents joined by or/nor, match pronoun number to nearest antecedent or recast sentence to avoid awkwardness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions and refinements to pronoun-number agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Refinements include: (1) two singular antecedents referring to same entity take singular pronoun; (2) antecedents modified by each/every/no take singular pronoun; (3) or/nor constructs treat antecedents separately; (4) when antecedents differ in number use nearest antecedent for agreement; (5) when joined by and, use plural pronoun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: (1) {a lawyer and role model received her recognition}; (2) {every college and university encourages its students to succeed}; (3) {neither the orange nor the peach smells as sweet as it should}; (4) recast sentence so plural antecedent comes last when useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pronouns with multiple antecedents — person precedence
rubrics_metrics.description: When a pronoun has antecedents of different persons connected by and/or/or/nor, the pronoun must take the person of one antecedent; preference order: first person > second person > third person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if antecedents are you and I, the following pronoun should be first person ({you or I should get to work on our experiment}). If antecedents are second and third person, use second ({you and she can settle your dispute}). If referring to just one antecedent, take that antecedent's person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pronoun case rules — nominative/objective/genitive/reflexive
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply case according to function: subject → nominative; object of verb/preposition → objective; possessive → genitive; reflexive when referring back to subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Four essential rules: (1) subject → nominative ({he is vice president}); (2) object of verb → objective ({she thanked him}); (3) object of preposition → objective ({please keep this between you and me}); (4) subject of an infinitive → objective ({does Tina want me to leave?}). Also note pronoun after linking verb traditionally nominative ({It was she}).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pronouns in apposition — case determined by syntactic function
rubrics_metrics.description: The case of a pronoun used in apposition follows the grammatical function (subject or object) of the words with which it is in apposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: {we three—Bruce, Felipe, and I—traveled...} (appositive in subjective function) vs {she asked us—Barbara, Sarah, and me—to move our cars} (appositive in object function).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid nominative-for-object errors in compound objects (common slip)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use nominative forms in compound objects (e.g., use me, not I: 'Read this and tell Laura and me'), check by removing the other element to see correct case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common incorrect forms: 'The test would be simple for you or I.' Correct: 'for you or me.' The foolproof check is to read the pronoun alone: 'tell me' vs 'tell I.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Classes of pronouns and multifunctionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Pronouns are categorized into classes—personal, demonstrative, reciprocal, interrogative, relative, indefinite, adjective—and many pronouns can function in more than one way depending on use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: that can be demonstrative, relative, or adjective depending on context. Knowledge of classes helps in analyzing and using pronouns correctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal pronoun forms and capitalisation (I always capitalized)
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal pronouns vary by person, number, and case; the first-person singular 'I' is always capitalized wherever it appears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference table of nominative/objective/genitive/reflexive forms provided. Remember that 'you' is singular and plural in form but always takes a plural verb in Modern English.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predicate nominative after linking verbs — nominative preferred
rubrics_metrics.description: A pronoun complement of a linking verb (predicate nominative) should traditionally be in the nominative case (This is he, not This is him).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In everyday speech 'This is him' is common, but formal usage maintains nominative case for predicate nominatives. The pronoun functioning as predicate nominative is termed an 'attribute pronoun.'
